items.title: Compliance with the 30-minute standard has never been measured
items.whyItMatters: The policy gives assurance without data, and the director's decision on escalation needs to know where delays occur.
items.opportunity: Measure compliance by location, time of day and analyte from two years of call logs.

items.title: The interval must be defined before analysis
items.whyItMatters: Studies measure timeliness from collection, verification or the first call, which gives different answers (claim c2).
items.opportunity: Measure from verification to documented read-back and treat a missing read-back as unsuccessful.

items.title: Results never successfully notified
items.whyItMatters: A result with no documented read-back is the most dangerous case and disappears if analysis uses only completed calls.
items.opportunity: Report never-notified results as a separate secondary outcome.

items.title: Community patients after hours carry the risk
items.whyItMatters: Patients at home, often in outlying areas, depend on a clinic that is closed.
items.opportunity: Report community after-hours results separately and by clinic area.

errorsFound: Staff accounts attribute delays mainly to night staffing; the retrieved evidence suggests unreachable clinicians for community results matter at least as much, so both must be measured.
reevaluation: The gaps confirm a retrospective review with a fixed interval definition, never-notified results reported separately and community results after hours as the key subgroup.
summary: Four gaps: unmeasured compliance, interval definition, never-notified results, and risk carried by community patients after hours.
